O V E R A L L   A P P R O A C H
LEAN SIX SIGMA ENABLES EDGE TO DEAL WITH INCREASING CUSTOMER REQUIREMENTS
Why Six Sigma?
• Create world class processes with little variation and 0 defects
• Enable highest quality in products and processes
• Cope with increasing complexity in products and services

What is Six Sigma?
• A holistic framework to define, structure and implement improvement projects
• A precisely defined approach following the five steps of the DMAIC cycle
• A structured method to solve complex problems and increase quality and efficiency
How to approach Six Sigma?
• Build a solid qualification basis within your employees
• Get buy-in from top management
• Define first Six Sigma projects and implement quickly to show the impact

THE EXTENDED DEFECT DEFINITION IN SIX SIGMA
Classic definition:
A defect exists when a defined quality requirement for a 
product feature is not met

Definition as understood by Six Sigma:
A defect also exists when a customer requirement for a 
product or service that has not been articulated is not 
met = dissatisfied customer
Merely fulfilling the contractually agreed services is not enough in a 0-defect 
culture. Even if a customer expectation that has not been articulated is not 
met, this is also considered a defect in Six Sigma.

occurred defects

action patterns working

Future QM approach requires 0-defect

A preventive approach 
dealing with defects

in terms of potential risks of error, e.g.:
• Risky ways of working and acting
• Risky processes and interfaces
• External risk factors such as 
suppliers and supply chains
• Risks of error due to specifications 
and decision premises of 
management
Advantage and solution:
Identify and reduce risks before the 
defects actually occurs

THE PRACTICAL AND STATISTICAL ARENA
SOLVING PROBLEMS WITH STATISTICS
• Taking the right measurements is crucial to finding the right solutions to practical 
problems
• Data-driven problem solving is an iterative process with roughly four steps (see

picture), moving from the practical arena to the statistical arena, and then 
returning to the practical arena with a conclusion in the following sequence:
1. Practical problem (practical arena)
2. Statistical problem (statistical arena)
3. Statistical solution (statistical arena)
4. Practical solution (practical arena)
• Each practical solution typically leads to further questions, starting a new iteration. 
These iterations may continue until the problem is resolved, and form the basis 
of a continuous process improvement program

VARIATION
• Variation can introduce waste and errors into a process. The more 
variation, the more errors and the more waste (see picture)
• Examples that are affected by variation are:
―The time that you arrive at work varies depending on traffic and route
―The number of potato chips in a bag varies depending on the size of 
each chip so that the net weight of the bag exceeds a minimum value

TYPES OF VARIATION THAT CONCERN A SIX SIGMA TEAM
• Common cause variation – All processes have common cause 
variation. This variation, also known as noise, is a normal part of any 
process. It demonstrates the true capability of a process
• Special cause variation – This variation is not normal to the process. It 
is the result of exceptions in the process environment
NOTE: 
•
In a process improvement project, special causes of variation should 
be the first target. Eliminating special causes of variation brings 
the process into a state of control and exposes the sources of 
common cause variation.

SIGMA LEVEL DESCRIPTION
• The Sigma Level determines the number of defects produced 
per million opportunities (DPMO) by any process 
• The higher the Sigma Level, the lesser are the defects produced
• It determines the number of defects and yield of the process and 
therefore is an indicator of quality
REASONS TO USE THE SIGMA LEVEL
• The Sigma Level is a high-level baseline metric, which helps to

understand the capability of the process. It can also be used to 
compare processes in an organization
• No process ever produces items that are exactly the same
• It shows the number of defects and yield of the process, 
ultimately pointing at the quality of the process
• It is the starting step to realizing the scope of improvement in any 
process
• Helps to visualize the difference between the current process 
curve and improved process curve

STEP 1: FIND THE DPMO*
DPMO* = (# of defects / # of opportunities) x 1,000,000
As per the example:

Hence, DPMO* = (750/150,000) x 1,000,000 = 5,000
The post office makes 5,000 defects per million opportunities
STEP 2: FIND THE YIELD OF THE PROCESS
Yield = ((# of opportunities – # of defects) / # opportunities) x 100
Again, as per the example:
Defects = 750
Opportunities = 150,000

Hence, Yield = (150,000 – 750 / 150,000) x 100 = 99.5%
The post office is producing with a yield of 99.5% in its 
processes

HISTOGRAMS ARE USED TO UNDERSTAND HOW THE OUTPUT OF A PROCESS RELATES TO CTQ AND HELP TO 
DETERMINE IF THE PROCESS IS CAPABLE MEETING CUSTOMER REQUIREMENTS

HISTOGRAM DESCRIPTION:
• Histograms are graphs of a distribution of data designed to show 
centering, dispersion (spread), and shape (relative frequency) of the data
Dispersion left
Dispersion right
REASONS TO USE A HISTOGRAM:
• Histograms are used to understand how the output of a process relates 
to CTQ (customer expectations, targets and specifications)
Bell-shaped curve
• Histograms help to determine if the process is capable meeting 
customer requirements
Central value
BENEFITS OF USING A HISTOGRAM:
• A histogram will show the central value of a characteristic produced by

your process, and the shape and size of the dispersion on either side of this 
central value
• The shape and size of the dispersion will help identify otherwise hidden 
sources of variation
• The data used to produce a histogram can ultimately be used to determine 
the capability of a process to produce output that consistently falls 
within specification limits

PARETO CHART DESCRIPTION
• A Pareto Chart is a vertical bar graph in which values are 
plotted in decreasing order of relative frequency from left to 
right
• The Pareto chart provides a graphic depiction of the Pareto 
principle, a theory maintaining that 80% of the output in a given 
situation or system is produced by 20% of the input

WHEN IS THE PARETO CHART USED 
•
In the Define phase of the DMAIC process to sort data and set 
priorities
In the Measure and Analyze phases to determine the relative 
value of items and to prioritize improvement actions
•
HOW TO CONSTRUCT A PARETO CHART
1. Gather data from the process by using a data tally or check 
and rank the items by putting the most frequent on top
2. Create the Pareto Chart. In the given example 80% of the 
problem can be found in physical and wiring defects. Therefore, 
if only those two aspects are worked on, the overall process 
could potentially improve by 80%

STATISTICAL PROCESS CONTROL (SPC) HAS BEEN INCORPORATED BY ORGANIZATIONS AROUND THE WORLD 
AS A PRIMARY TOOL TO IMPROVE PRODUCT QUALITY BY REDUCING PROCESS VARIATION

STATISTICAL PROCESS CONTROL FACTS
• The concepts of Statistical Process Control (SPC) were initially developed by Dr. Walter Shewhart of Bell Laboratories in the 
late 1920’s
• Expanded by by Dr. W. Edwards Deming, who introduced SPC to Japanese industry after WWII
• Statistical Process Control has now been incorporated by organizations around the world as a primary tool to improve product 
quality by reducing process variation
• There are two sources of process variation:
―Common Cause Variation that is inherent in the process, and stable over time

―Special Cause (or ‘uncontrolled’ variation, which is unstable over time - the result of specific events outside the system
• Reasons to use SPC:
―To separate special cause from common cause variation
―To detect trends and patterns in data that provide clues about the sources of variation (with the ultimate goal of reducing 
or eliminating those sources)
• You can think of control charts as expressing the ’Voice of the Process’

variable—that is not included in your analysis
• Regression Analysis is used in conjunction with 
correlation calculations and scatter plots to predict future 
performance based on past results
If a relationship does exist between X and Y on a scatter

CORRELATION AND REGRESSION VISUALIZATION
CORRELATION AND REGRESSION ANALYSIS DESCRIPTION
• Regression Analysis is used when it is hypothesized that one variable is dependent upon 
either: 
― Another single independent or input variable (Simple Regression) 
― Multiple independent or input variables (Multiple Regression)
• Simple Regression plots a line of best fit to the data of the form: Y = a + bX + e*

• A statistical measurement of correlation can be calculated using the Least Squares 
method (a mathematical routine) to quantify the strength of the relationship between two 
variables
• The output of that calculation is the Pearson’s Correlation Coefficient (r), which 
ranges between -1 and 1 
― A value of 1 indicates perfect positive correlation - as one variable increases, the 
second increases proportionally in a linear fashion 
― Likewise, a value of -1 indicates perfect negative correlation - as one variable

increases, the second decreases proportionally
― A value of zero indicates that there is no correlation between the two variables

BRAINSTORMING IS A TEAM-CENTERED PROCESS USED TO GENERATE NEW AND CREATIVE IDEAS TO SOLVE A 
PROBLEM
BRAINSTORMING DESCRIPTION
• Brainstorming is about creating an atmosphere of suspended judgment - no criticism - so that a large number of ideas freely 
flow from the participants
• The brainstorming session can be structured so that everyone participates in turn, or can be unstructured, with people given the

opportunity to participate at any time
STRUCTURED BRAINSTORMING- ENCOURAGE EQUAL PARTICIPATION
1. After forming the team, the problem to be solved is stated and written down for everyone to see
2. Moving around the room, each team member offers an idea (ensure there is no criticism of ideas)
3. The team leader or a designated person records the ideas as they are generated on the flipchart or whiteboard
4. Keep moving around the room until there are no ideas left.
5. Review the list of ideas to make sure they are clearly worded, and eliminate duplicate ideas
6. Group or combine ideas if there are natural categories

UNSTRUCTURED BRAINSTORMING- SPONTANEOUS FREE FLOW OF IDEAS
• The unstructured process follows the outline above with one difference - ideas are offered by anyone at any time rather than by 
ordered rotation around the room

BENCHMARKING IS THE PROCESS OF DEVELOPING NEW AND HIGHER PERFORMANCE TARGETS AND 
STANDARDS FOR YOUR PROCESS BASED ON A COMPARISON TO OTHER PROCESSES
BENCHMARKING EXAMPLE
BENCHMARKING DESCRIPTION
• The objective of Benchmarking is to find examples of superior 
performance and understand the processes and practices driving 
that performance
• Benchmarking improves performance by identifying and applying 
best demonstrated practices to operations, sales and other 
processes
• Companies then improve their performance by tailoring and

incorporating these best practices into their own operations—not 
by imitating, but by innovating

• Hospital A decides to benchmark its registration process 
with Hospital B, who demonstrates a better performance 
in terms of less errors, faster cycle time and greater 
customer satisfaction
• Hospital A can learn from Hospital B and then improve 
its performance by setting higher targets and reinventing 
their registration process to make it better 
B E N C H M A R K I N G
T Y P E S
THERE ARE FOUR GENERAL TYPES OF BENCHMARKING METHODS AND SEVERAL SOURCES FOR DATA 
GATHERING AND COMPARISON
BENCHMARKING TYPES

SOURCES FOR BENCHMARKING
1. Internal benchmarking is a comparison 
of a business process to a similar process 
inside the organization
2. Competitive benchmarking is a direct 
competitor-to-competitor comparison of a 
product, service, process, or method
3. Functional benchmarking is a 
comparison to similar or identical practices 
within the same or similar functions outside 
the immediate industry
4. Generic benchmarking broadly 
conceptualizes unrelated business 
processes or functions that can be 
practiced in the same or similar ways 
regardless of the industry.

1. Facility Visits
Many companies provide facility tours and are willing to share their success stories. 
2. Company Publications
These have information about employment levels and production output. Rough 
measures of productivity can be made through this
3. Industry Publications & Trade Journals
Publications such as Industry Week offer feature articles which often contain 
performance metrics
4. Third Party Studies
Market research reports are a valuable sources due to their objectivity and detail

5. Public Financial Reports
Financial filings and annual reports are readily available and provide financial 
benchmarks 
6. Tear-Downs
A competitors product can be teared down to understand the components used which 
gives benchmarks on size, weight, build etc. 
7. Books
Many books have benchmarking information. Some have detailed case studies on lean 
manufacturing examples with hard benchmark data

FAILURE MODE AND EFFECTS ANALYSIS (FMEA) IS A TOOL USED TO PRIORITIZE POTENTIAL DEFECTS BASED 
ON THEIR SEVERITY, EXPECTED FREQUENCY, AND LIKELIHOOD OF DETECTION
FAILURE MODE AND EFFECTS ANAYLSIS EXAMPLE
Example of a simplified FMEA for a seat belt installation process at an 
automobile assembly plant:
As shown, three potential failure modes have been identified.  Failure mode

FAILURE MODE AND EFFECTS ANAYLSIS DESCRIPTION
• FMEA is used to prompt actions to improve design or process 
robustness 
• The FMEA highlights weaknesses in the current design process in 
•
terms of the customer 
It is an excellent vehicle to prioritize and organize continuous 
improvement efforts on areas which offer the greatest return
ADVANTAGES OF USING FMEA
• The FMEA is a matrix that establishes priorities based on the risk 
of failure
• Scores are assigned to each potential defect mode of a process

in three categories:
― Severity: The seriousness of a failure mode
― Occurrence: The likelihood that a given failure mode will 
happen
― Detection: The likelihood that a given failure mode will be 
detected if it occurs, prior to release to a customer 
• A combined score of the above, conveys the overall risk of a 
customer problem, called the Risk Priority Number, or RPN
• The worst case is represented by those defects which are severe, 
likely to occur, and hard to detect
PUBLIC
• Greater the RPN, higher is the priority for improvement

OVERALL EQUIPMENT EFFECTIVENESS – OEE; BACKGROUND
•
•
•
•
•
•
The concept of OEE belongs to Lean Management and is used as a meaningful performance measure metric which 
calculates the net value generated by the machine

This measure has been developed by Seiichi Nakajima, working for the Japan Institute for Plant Maintenance (JIPM) in 
1960‘s within the context of TPM
The meaning of the OEE is a kind of relationship between the best possible effectiveness and the effectiveness factually 
realized in practice
It not only gives you the picture the current effectiveness of the used machines, the OEE also delivers transparency 
about drivers of the losses 
Therefore the OEE focusses on 3 sub-criteria for evaluation:

 Machine Availability
 Machine Performance 
 Output Quality
Finally, the OEE is calculated as the product of the results related to the aforementioned criterions

Audit: Definition and explanation
• The noun audit comes from the Latin verb "audire", meaning to

listen. The noun also exists in English. 
• Audit stands for a general examination procedure that examines 
products and processes with regard to the fulfilment of specific 
criteria. 
• The audit is therefore always based on a defined reference in terms 
of the criteria to be fulfilled and verifies the degree of compliance
in relation to the company's actual practice.
• Layered Audits are very relevant in the shop floor
• They engage all organizational levels of the shopfloor 
management in Self-Audits and may be relevant drivers of the 
continuous improvement process, such as

• 5S-Audits
• Audits on compliance to standardized work
• Audits on compliance with TPM standards
